name: Aaron Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aaron, 58, a senior developer and team lead at a small tech company that makes ambulance dispatch maps. I have a master's degree and know the road exceptions well, although our pay scale is below bigger firms and few software employers are close. I have never used AI tools; a dispatcher's written correction tells me when a night gate is locked. My partner sews for customers at home, our sons are grown, and we rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell dispatchers a caller's location has to match the road the ambulance can reach. I lead software fixes for a tech company's dispatch-map app and have never used AI; I listen to the recorded route correction before changing a junction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even with AI mostly quiet, the rent worries me. I have a master's degree and lead the team, yet this small firm pays below the usual senior rate; my partner's sewing orders vary, we have two weeks saved, and there are few similar software jobs here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking wrong-turn tickets against dispatcher route notes. We'd cancel the 31 monthly sports package and put the fee into a rent account whenever both incomes arrive, then check the rent date before buying extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A quiet machine future does not make a variable sewing order arrive on payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was wrong with the route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An ambulance was routed through a gate locked at night. The dispatcher knew the service road was open, and I changed the map after checking the crew's written route note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons cover rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown sons have work and bills elsewhere. I want them to call home, not become our rent plan.

I'd keep **locked gates** out of ambulance directions.
think: I have **two weeks saved** despite a team-lead title.
I earn **below senior market pay** with few software jobs nearby.

feel: **Anxious** about rent and uneven sewing income before AI changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could write map code and answer location questions, but a locked gate must not become an ambulance route. I want a dispatcher to be able to reject a bad turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead experience might keep me in the room, but the firm could cut the hours spent maintaining ordinary streets. Two weeks saved and irregular sewing pay give us little time to adjust if my own hours shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a list of blocked-gate corrections and ask the ambulance service for its monthly route-error meeting notes. We would postpone replacing our washing machine while it still runs; I'd check for actual paid route-review vacancies, but apply only if combined income covers rent, food and travel without assuming a full month of sewing orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours. I am not going to put an AI-generated route on a live ambulance map without a tested way for a dispatcher to stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which two routes must be compared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The night-gate case and the open service road need to be tested together. A map that avoids the gate by sending the ambulance into a closed yard has not solved the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the washer wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The washer rattles but works. We can keep the money until my paid hours are clear instead of using the rent buffer for a newer machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write dispatch code before ambulance robots arrive around 2031. A human still needs to say the bridge is shut when the map is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead post could be removed quickly if software makes and checks routes cheaply. My partner's sewing orders do not cover rent reliably, and two weeks saved would vanish before I found another senior job in this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the ambulance service and two nearby tech firms about actual paid call-support, route-review or software openings and written wages and shifts. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed post whose wage with conservative sewing income covers rent, food and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek any available paid local work and contact our landlord before rent is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A senior title cannot buy three months of rent when the payslip stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show an employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a hiring manager the locked-gate correction without the caller's name or address. The dispatcher route note explains why the service road was safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which sewing income would you use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would use the lowest recent sewing month in the calculation, not the best. If new night shifts stop my partner from taking paid orders, the signed wage alone must meet the bills.

I'd check **signed paid openings** before promising another job.

steps.text: Ask ambulance service and two tech firms about paid support or route-review jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives time to learn what the ambulance service actually asks of a human call taker. Thinking AI reaches my code first, and hands-on robots would follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to move from software into calls, but I have never answered a live emergency line. I cannot pay for a course or leave my wage for an unpaid training place with only two weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the service for its paid call-taker selection rules, shift pattern and course pay. If a real place opens, the service funds training on paid hours, and the training wage with conservative sewing income covers rent, food and travel even if night shifts reduce orders, I'd enrol; after 2031 I'd take a signed call-taker job only on those terms, otherwise keep paid coding while available and seek other local paid work if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years lets me see a training rota rather than imagine one. A course brochure is not a dispatch headset or a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course need to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course would need supervised practice on a blocked-gate call and a caller who cannot name the street. I would not treat my map knowledge as proof I can talk a frightened person through an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would night shifts affect sewing work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner wants the night rota before I apply. If I am away when sewing orders are collected, we need to price the lost orders rather than pretend they still arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 might take me to 68, but thinking AI would reach dispatch code before ambulance robots around 2039. Someone on the phone still has to hear a caller say the bridge is closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still have two weeks saved today and no checked pension figure. My partner's sewing orders vary, so a long warning does not make the current rent secure by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the blocked-gate log and save the cancelled 31 sports fee whenever both incomes arrive, then request both retirement statements and compare verified amounts with the lowest recent sewing months and our rent. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if verified income covers rent, food and travel; otherwise I'd keep or seek available paid local work without counting our sons' wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about rent, even with ten years on the card. I do not want to retire on the memory of a good sewing month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which months would you compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The statements need a monthly amount and start date. We would put them beside the rent and the last six sewing months, not a best-case order book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons help financially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our sons can come for supper, but they are building their own homes. Their wages are theirs, and our retirement calculation should say so.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the main dispatch-code wage could go before another paid local post appears. Written cut notice, real shift wages and early landlord contact would help us keep rent current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what a good route looks like after midnight. A locked gate stays locked even if a map draws a straight line through it; the crew needs the open road.

headlineQuote: A locked gate stays locked even if a map draws a straight line through it; the crew needs the open road.
portrait: Aaron, **58**, leads ambulance-map software after a master's degree and checks night routes against dispatcher notes.
His **lower senior pay**, partner's variable sewing orders, two-week reserve and few nearby software firms make rent precarious now.
He has **never used AI** and keeps blocked-gate corrections and dispatcher veto ahead of an automatic route.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** him; signed replacement pay must cover bills even if night shifts stop sewing orders.
A five-year call-taker path requires **funded paid training**, supervised practice, qualifying wages and shifts; retirement needs verified income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his lead wage before another paid dispatch role appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, real shift wages and landlord contact before arrears would help protect rent.
